[1] ROOT CAUSE, RESTATED PRECISELY. `wait_for_phase`, `get_current_phase` and
    `next_market_open` each independently called `now_et()` — up to five unsynchronized
    clock reads per loop iteration. Today's incident is the proof, not an inference: the
    bot's own log line showed `current_phase: "market_open"` (a late read) alongside
    `wait_seconds: 3600` (committed from an earlier read that still saw pre-market, whose
    branch treats "today's open already passed" as certain and hands off to
    `next_market_open()` for TOMORROW's open). No re-check before the `await`.

[2] FIX IS STRUCTURAL, NOT A PATCH OF THE ONE BRANCH THAT FIRED. `get_current_phase()` and
    `next_market_open()` both gained an optional `now: datetime | None = None` parameter —
    the SAME precedent already in this codebase (`orchestrator._post_stop_cooldown_cutoff`,
    W21). `wait_for_phase` now captures exactly ONE `now = now_et()` per loop iteration and
    threads it through every decision in that iteration: the phase check, both boundary
    comparisons, `next_market_open(now)`, and the log line's `current_phase`
    (`self.get_current_phase(now).value`, not a fresh call). An early return the instant that
    single read already satisfies the target means the contradictory branch can no longer
    execute in that case — not "less likely", structurally unreachable.

## 2026-09-16 - W22 FOLLOW-UP: two UX gaps found by actually using it, both closed same-day
Not new findings from review — the operator declared both real positions, then immediately
hit two rough edges that only using the feature (not reading the code) would surface.

[1] THE HALT DIDN'T LIFT ON ANSWERING. Both real positions were declared "yes" (12:17 and
    12:44 ET), but HALT_UNTRACKED only clears on the NEXT reconcile() pass — which under the
    original design meant waiting for post-market, tomorrow's pre-market, or another restart.
    `TradingOrchestrator.reconcile_now()` runs one pass on demand; the poller fires it (as a
    background task, never awaited inline) immediately after recording an answer. Kept
    deliberately decoupled: the poller still holds no broker reference of its own, so a slow
    or failed reconcile can never block it from processing the NEXT inbound update, and
    reconcile_now catches its own errors so a broken callback can't take the poller down.

[2] THE CONFIRMATION WASN'T VISIBLE. The operator tapped both buttons, then asked whether
    their reply was received — the actual answer (edited prompt text) was there, but it was

## 2026-09-16 - W23 EXECUTED + DEPLOYED: the scheduler's silent timezone fallback, closed
Confirmed live at 09-13-16 09:35 ET (digest_am firing at 03:35 ET), registered across three
sessions, finally probed to precision and fixed today.

[1] THREE BUGS, NOT ONE — each confirmed by direct probe against this box's real apscheduler
    3.11.2, not assumed from the API surface, and each needing a DIFFERENT fix:
    (a) Nine pre-built `CronTrigger(...)` objects never inherited the scheduler's own
        `timezone="US/Eastern"` — apscheduler only injects that when IT builds a trigger from an
        alias string ("cron"); a pre-built object keeps `get_localzone()` at construction time
        (probed: Europe/Madrid, this host). Fixed with explicit `timezone=ET` on all nine.
    (b) The two naive `run_date=` catch-up jobs are a DIFFERENT mechanism, easy to conflate with
        (a) but confirmed distinct: a naive datetime through the `"date"` alias is MISLABELED
        with the scheduler's offset, not converted — probed fresh today, naive `20:38:13` (real
        host wall clock) came back labeled `20:38:13-04:00`, an instant 6h in the future.
        Live-evidence match: `retrain_catchup` registered `21:31:45 EDT`, ran `03:31:45` local.
        An AWARE `run_date` passes through byte-for-byte unchanged — probed and now a permanent
        regression test, not just a plan-time claim.
    (c) `_backtest_catchup_run_at`'s own market-hours-avoidance check compared naive-host-local
        hours against ET thresholds (9:15/16:30) — the wrong clock, independent of what the
        scheduler later did with the result.

[2] DELIBERATELY UNCHANGED, and the reason is now load-bearing, not incidental:
    `_backtest_catchup_due`'s naive-local `now` stays naive — its own prior docstring already
    explained this is intentional (compared against equally-naive file mtimes; a naive
    Sunday-20:00 slot is immaterial for a coarse weekly gate). Fixing (b)/(c) means the SAME
    catch-up now passes TWO deliberately different clocks to two sibling functions — the
    due-check keeps naive `datetime.now()`, the run-at computation gets a fresh `now_et()`. A
    comment at the call site says so explicitly, and a dedicated test
    (`test_call_site_uses_two_different_clocks_not_one`) checks the SOURCE keeps them separate —
    the exact kind of "helpful simplification" that would silently reintroduce (c).

[3] THE RETRAIN CATCH-UP FIX REUSED AN ALREADY-AWARE CLOCK RATHER THAN READING A NEW ONE.
    `_now_c` (the retrain due-check's own clock) was ALREADY `now_et()` under a local alias —
    only the separate `_rt_at = datetime.now() + timedelta(minutes=2)` was naive. Fixed by
    reusing `_now_c` for the new `_retrain_catchup_run_at(_now_c)` call instead of reading the
    clock a second time — one `now` per decision, the same discipline W24 established for the
    market-open race.

[4] TESTS — new file, 14 tests, zero prior coverage of this exact class existed (though
    `_backtest_catchup_due`/`_backtest_catchup_run_at` had none dedicated either before today).
    An AST scan of `main()`'s source catches a future 10th `CronTrigger` site missing the fix —
    this codebase's own established rule (W20's `hour_of_day`, W21's 19-vs-18 reader count were
    BOTH found this way, not by re-checking known-fixed sites). Real execution against a real
    `BlockingScheduler`, not just the keyword's presence: `daily_report`'s next fire time,
    computed from a known instant, lands on 16:30 ET, not 10:30. NEGATIVE CONTROLS proving the
    underlying bugs are real, not just that the fix's shape looks plausible — the same
    `CronTrigger(...)` call WITHOUT `timezone=` resolves to something other than `US/Eastern`;
    the same naive `run_date` through the same alias comes back mislabeled, reproducing the
    exact 6h-late live incident as a permanent regression test. Both market-hours boundary
    instants (9:15 and 16:30 ET) exercised directly, not just interior points.
    Suite: 1811 passed / 43 skipped / 1 known local-.env failure — up from 1797, no regressions.

[5] DEPLOY. Full supervisor restart (master.py IS the supervisor). Clean shutdown (~31s), clean

The last major unclaimed item, deferred through W17, W18, W19, W20 and effectively every wave

[1] SCOPE, MEASURED BEFORE PLANNING rather than assumed. Universe = **206**: R24's own 109
    standing findings + 78 carried-over OPEN from the prior register + 19 R24-marked PARTIAL.
    HONEST COUNT DISCREPANCY, stated rather than absorbed: R24's header says it triaged "123
    prior findings" but its triage section holds **126** rows (78 OPEN + 19 PARTIAL + 28 FIXED
    + 1 OBSOLETE). Three rows unaccounted for. NOT resolved; carried forward.

[2] WHY BATCHED, and this is the number that shaped the whole approach. Only 22 of 109 R24
    findings are mentioned anywhere in PLAN.md after R24 was written; ZERO of the 78 carried-over
    ones are; only 17 of 109 carry a fix-marker comment in `src/` or `tests/`. So **165 of 187
    have no trace at all** across ten days and ~18 waves. There is no grep shortcut — the
    fix-marker convention is real but is a LOWER bound on what's closed, never an upper one.
    Closing 206 in one pass would either burn many sessions with nothing durable in between or
    silently degrade into skimming, which is worse than not doing it: a wrongly-closed finding
    is a live defect marked safe.

[3] THE METHOD ASYMMETRY, which is what makes the output trustworthy. Marking OPEN is cheap —
    re-read the cited `Where:` and see whether the claim still holds. Marking CLOSED must be
    expensive: the fix in code AND a test that pins it. A wrongly-OPEN finding costs a re-check;
    a wrongly-CLOSED one retires a real defect in silence.

## 2026-09-17 - W26 EXECUTED — the entry-budget give-back + the cluster-scoped cooldown

(b) from the W25 pointer, both findings from register-triage batch 1, both on the live entry path.
Register-don't-fix does not apply to the two named findings. STAGED, NOT DEPLOYED.

[1] data-integrity-07 — FIXED, and LATENT rather than materialized, measured before planning.
    The live DB has ZERO `stale_pending_never_filled` rows; 10 trades placed, 10 closed, and
    `daily_stats.trades_taken` reads 5 + 5 — matching exactly. So the counter has never actually
    been wrong in the live record. Worth fixing anyway, and the consequence is larger now than when
    it was found: the first-hour budget is 2, so ONE phantom halves first-hour capacity.
    The sweep (`reconciler._sweep_stale_pending`) now calls a new `_refund_entry_budget` when it
    books a never-filled close. Three correctness points, each of which would make this a WORSE bug
    than the one being fixed if got wrong:
      (a) GATED ON THE CAS. `close_trade` returns "True iff the close landed" and the sweep
          DISCARDED it, then ran `closed += 1` unconditionally — so a lost CAS was already being
          miscounted as a close. A refund on that path would credit a slot back for an order that
          actually FILLED. Now captured; on False it refunds nothing, counts nothing, and logs
          `sweep_close_lost_cas`.
      (b) THE TRADE'S OWN ENTRY DATE, never today. `reconcile()` runs on every startup, so a
          phantom placed Monday is typically swept Tuesday morning. Crediting TODAY would hand back
          a slot today never spent, and `taken = -1` makes `_get_trade_budget` return
          `max_trades + 1` — a FAIL-OPEN on the daily cap, produced by a data-integrity fix.
      (c) FLOORED AT 0. A negative counter inflates the budget the same way. W25 shipped the
          mirror image of this lesson (a floor of 1 manufacturing a position where 0 was correct):
          a floor is only safe in the direction that cannot create permission.
    REJECTED ALTERNATIVE, recorded because it is the obvious one: move the increment to
    fill-confirmation so the counter only counts real trades. The budget's purpose is pacing
    PLACEMENT (2 in the first hour, 4 by mid-day); counting only fills lets a whole scan cycle place
    orders before any fill, bypassing the tiers entirely. Same shape as W25's rejected `max(0,...)`
    — the tidier-looking fix changes trading behaviour.

[2] logic-exit-risk-03 — FIXED, with a DELIBERATE DEVIATION from the literal spec, stated here
    rather than left to read as a faithful implementation.
    One authority now: `correlation.symbol_clusters()` / `cluster_symbols()`. The fact lived in
    three shapes before — `CorrelationGuard._same_sector_cluster` (pairwise),
    `RiskManager._count_correlated_positions` (re-inlining the intersection off a direct
    SECTOR_GROUPS import), and NOT AT ALL in the cooldown, which is the defect. Both existing
    consumers delegate. The delegation is deliberately NOT `sym2 in cluster_symbols(sym1)`:
    cluster_symbols() always contains the symbol itself, which would make
    `_same_sector_cluster("GLD","GLD")` True where the original is False — unreachable through
    check_correlation today (the `existing == new_symbol` arm short-circuits) but an exact
    delegation cannot be broken by a future caller that does reach it. Pinned by a test.
    THE WINDOW IS GRADUATED, and this is the operator decision of the wave: the stopped symbol keeps
    the full R12-B4 one-trading-day window; cluster SIBLINGS get
    `risk.post_stop_cluster_cooldown_minutes` (default 120, `0` disables and restores the exact
    pre-W26 behaviour without a code change). Strict cluster-wide scoping — the finding as written —
    would darken the ENTIRE BOOK, because the universe is a single cluster, for the rest of the
    session AND all of the next (a Monday 14:00 stop clears only Wednesday: Tuesday's cutoff is
    Monday 09:30). With a touch stop as the primary loss exit and a volume-tuned config
    (max_daily_trades 12, min_confidence 0.50, 1 contract "= max # of trades") that is close to
    "the first stop ends the trading day". The hazard R12-B4 actually targets is IMMEDIATE re-entry
    into the same adverse move — the live 08-24 QQQ instance was 13 minutes. So: faithful for the
    stopped symbol, shorter for siblings. THIS DEVIATES from the spec's "one trading day" for
    siblings; a future reader should treat 120 as a tunable, not as R12-B4.
    The verdict return type changed from a bare exit_time to `CooldownBlock(symbol, exit_time)`
    because the blocking symbol is no longer necessarily the blocked one — an operator reading
    "QQQ entry blocked" otherwise has no way to see that a SPY stop caused it. The log now carries
    `stopped_symbol` and `via_cluster`.

[3] AN EXISTING TEST ASSERTED THE DEFECT, and was split rather than deleted.
    `test_r21_post_stop_cooldown.py::test_other_symbol_unaffected` asserted that a QQQ touch stop
    does NOT block SPY — which is precisely logic-exit-risk-03. The assertion was not wrong so much
    as under-specified: what it protected is that an UNRELATED symbol is not swept up, and SPY/QQQ
    were a poor example of "unrelated". Replaced by `test_unrelated_symbol_unaffected` using GLD
    (in no SECTOR_GROUPS set) with sibling scoping ON; the sibling case is pinned in the new file.
    That file's `_orch()` helper also had to start carrying Settings, and its comment claiming it
    "touches no orchestrator state besides the DB file" was corrected. It defaults to
    sibling_minutes=0 so every other test in it keeps measuring exactly what R12-B4/R22 wrote it to
    measure.

[4] MY OWN PLAN'S ITEM 3 WAS WRONG BY 16x, and the guard was NOT shipped.

## 2026-09-17 - W27 EXECUTED — the credit floor at initial placement (regress-live-06)

(a) from the W26 pointer, and the LAST of the six confirmed-OPEN batch-1 findings. It was ranked
"most delicate" because it touches live entry pricing, so it got its own wave. STAGED, NOT DEPLOYED.

[1] CONFIRMED BY BOTH LENSES, AND SHARPER THAN THE REGISTER STATES.
    The register's claim is correct as far as it goes: `_credit_floors_hold` (executor.py) is called
    only from the reprice ladder, and the initial-placement path in `_execute_multi_leg` had no
    floor check. Probing it produced two facts the register does not contain:
      (a) A SIGNAL SITTING EXACTLY ON THE FLOOR ALWAYS BREACHED — with a perfectly fresh quote and
          no adverse move. `combo_entry_limit`'s offset has a 10c MINIMUM, so step 0 concedes 2.5c
          unconditionally: a $0.70 signal was placed at $0.67. This is not a tail case, it is EVERY
          MARGINAL SIGNAL — precisely the trades the floor exists to filter. The register reads as
          though the breach needs an adverse move; it does not.
      (b) THE SYSTEM REFUSED AT REPRICE EXACTLY WHAT IT ACCEPTED AT PLACEMENT. Probed directly:
          `_credit_floors_hold(pending, -0.67)` returns False for the very price the placement path
          put on the wire unchecked. The guard was correct all along and simply was never wired to
          the ladder's FIRST and LARGEST concession.
    Compounding both: the pricing anchor is the LIVE MID, not the signal's validated credit, and the
    staleness gate admits a mid up to 35% away — so the worst case the gates permit is ~30% below
    the floor ($0.70 signal placed at $0.49).

[2] THE FIX, and both halves mirror guards that ALREADY EXISTED on sibling paths rather than
    inventing a new policy:
      - REFUSE when `_base_mag < floor_min`: the market's own mid cannot pay the economics that
        justified the signal, so the premise is void. CAS PENDING->CANCELLED and return None — the
        same shape as the disorderly-spread and stale-signal refusals a few lines above.
      - CLAMP otherwise: raise the limit magnitude to the floor so step 0 never concedes below it.
        The same shape as the debit side's `_debit_cap`, which has had this protection since R8.
        Safe by construction: on a credit, demanding MORE credit can never make an order more
        aggressive than it already was.
    ENTRIES ONLY, and this is the detail that could have made this wave a disaster:
    `_execute_multi_leg` SERVES EXITS TOO. The floors describe the economics that justify OPENING a
    position; applying them to a close would refuse or reprice the exit of a losing trade — the
    exact inversion of protection, and a missed exit is the worst outcome this system has. The gate
    is `is_credit and not is_exit`, and two tests pin that exits are untouched in both directions
    (still placed, and NOT repriced to the entry floor).

[3] TWO NEW SINGLE AUTHORITIES, because placement and reprice must never drift again:
    `_credit_floor_minimum(width)` (max(min_credit, min_ratio*width); min_credit when width<=0,
    preserving `_credit_floors_hold`'s pre-W27 semantics exactly) and `_wing_width_from_legs(legs)`.
    The width split was FORCED by the defect's own shape: at placement time NO PendingOrder exists
    yet — the caller builds it only after `place_order` returns — so the check there has a signal
    and its legs and nothing else. `_pending_wing_width` keeps its trade-row legs-JSON fallback
    (meaningful only there) and delegates the arithmetic. Verified the persisted legs JSON always
    carries `expiry`, which `_leg_fields` requires, before routing the fallback through it.

[4] PROVEN LOAD-BEARING, NOT MERELY GREEN. A suite that passes proves nothing about a guard unless
    its absence fails. Neutralising `_credit_floor_minimum` at runtime (returning 0.0, i.e. the
    pre-W27 behaviour) reproduces the defect EXACTLY through the real `execute_signal`:
    `placed=[0.67]` with the floor off, `placed=[0.70]` with the real code.

[5] REGISTERED, NOT FIXED (operator decision), in `reports/register_triage_20260916.md` under
    "W27 ADDENDUM": 22 `AIT_*` keys are read via raw `os.environ.get` in `src/` and **21 are absent
    from CONTRACT_DEFAULTS**. A distinction I would have missed by trusting my own first number, so
    it is recorded rather than smoothed over: **16** carry a COMPETING FALLBACK LITERAL — the actual
    R19c violation ("no production module may carry a private default for a contract key") — while
    **5 are bare presence reads** with no competing default and are a weaker case, listed separately
    rather than inflating the headline count.
    THE STRUCTURAL POINT, worth more than the list: `test_no_raw_environ_reads_of_contract_keys`
    BUILDS ITS REGEX FROM `CONTRACT_DEFAULTS`, so it polices only keys already registered and is
    blind to every key that never was. That is the same guard-hole shape as W26 [4]'s `date.today()`
    finding, and the pattern deserves naming: **a class guard keyed on a registry cannot catch what
    was never registered.** The load-bearing members are not hygiene —
    `AIT_IC_DELTA_MIN`/`MAX` and `AIT_IRON_CONDOR_IV_FLOOR` decide STRIKE SELECTION and entry gating
    for the only live strategy, `AIT_CREDIT_TOUCH_STOP` arms the primary loss exit,
    `AIT_IV_RANK_CAP`/`AIT_MAX_PER_EXPIRY` are risk gates, `AIT_ALLOW_AFTER_HOURS` gates
    market-hours enforcement — each with a private default `config.yaml` cannot override and the
    divergence report cannot see. The wing_k incident R19 was written about is the same shape.
    W27 does not depend on any of it: the clamp binds whatever `AIT_ENTRY_LADDER_START` is set to.

[6] VERIFICATION. `tests/test_w27_credit_floor_at_placement.py`, 23 tests, reusing the established
    builders in `test_w2_executor_risk_gates.py` (real executor, real StateManager on a tmp DB, only
    the broker boundary faked).
    - NEGATIVE CONTROL: reconstructs the pre-W27 step-0 arithmetic and asks the UNCHANGED reprice
      guard what it thinks of that price — it refuses. The asymmetry in one test. Asserts the
      premise ($0.70 -> $0.67) first so it cannot pass vacuously.
    - EXIT SAFETY in both directions (see [2]).
    - CLASS GUARD: over a 12-case credit x width grid, every limit the placement path emits must
      satisfy `_credit_floors_hold` — the general form of the defect (an entry priced without
      consulting the floor), not the one line that caused it.
    - AN ANTI-VACUITY GUARD ON THAT GUARD, because the drift test passes trivially for any case it
      refuses: 8 of the 12 grid cases must actually place an order, so a future change that made the
      floor refuse everything cannot turn the suite green while placing nothing.
    - Gates: full fast lane **1882 passed / 43 skipped / 1 failed** (the known local-`.env`
      `test_r19_config_authority` case). Reconciled: 1859 + 23 = 1882. `compileall` OK,
      `scripts/typecheck.py` OK, `scripts/smoke_deploy.py` SMOKE PASS (13 checks).

The first half of the combined census wave. Operator decision: fix all 49 `date.today()` sites now,

[1] SEVERITY, MEASURED — AND THIS CORRECTS MY OWN W26 ENTRY.
    I pinned the host to Europe/Berlin and swept the clock rather than reasoning about it. **The
    entire RTH session (09:30-16:00 ET = 15:30-22:00 CEST) falls inside the band where the host date
    and the ET date AGREE.** Divergence is 18:00-24:00 ET only.
    So the live scan/exit loops were NEVER wrong on this host. W26 [4] called this finding
    "UNCONDITIONAL, not fault-gated — every evening evaluation is already wrong" and used that to
    rank it above the batch-3 fail-open sites. The first clause is true; the ranking inference was
    OVER-STATED, because the evaluations that matter do not happen in the evening. Recorded here
    rather than quietly re-ranked: a register entry that oversells is the same failure as one that
    undersells, and this ledger is where that gets corrected.
    WHAT WAS REALLY WRONG: the 18:00-24:00 ET window. Every evening restart this session — 19:08 and
    19:27 ET on 09-16 — ran startup reconcile and `_launch_size_coherence_check` against TOMORROW's
    date. That is the live instance, and it is ours.
    WHY FIX ALL 49 ANYWAY: the correctness is ACCIDENTAL. It holds only because the offset is +6. A
    host at ET+13 puts RTH itself across the date line and the live path IS wrong. Same shape as
    W25's cap-grid skew — contained by coincidence, not design.

[2] THE FIX. New `ait.utils.time.today_et()`, one named authority, and all 49 sites converted.
    Named rather than open-coded as `now_et().date()` for the reason W26/W27 both used, and for one
    more: it lets the guard forbid `.today()` OUTRIGHT, with **zero allowlist**. That is the whole
    argument for doing all 49 rather than a subset — a guard carrying 49 documented exceptions is a
    catalogue, which is precisely why W26 declined to ship this check against a partly-fixed tree.
    `utils/time.py` imports nothing from `ait`, so it is a leaf and the 16 new imports cannot create
    a cycle — checked before relying on it.

[3] ONE SITE WAS NOT A MECHANICAL SWAP, as the plan predicted. `ml/trainer.py` compares today's date
    against one recovered from `datetime.fromtimestamp(f.stat().st_mtime)` — naive host-local.
    Converting only the comparison side would subtract an ET date from a host-local one:
    re-introducing the mixed-convention defect W21 spent a whole wave removing, via the fix meant to
    prevent it. Both sides now read ET. Verified `min(candidates)` can never see a naive/aware MIX
    (the mtime path only runs when the list is empty), so no TypeError was introduced.
    AND THE INVERSE, recorded because it is the more dangerous half: the OTHER 9 `fromtimestamp`
    sites (master.py x5, ops_health.py x3, meta_label.py x1) are `datetime.now() - fromtimestamp(...)`
    — naive minus naive, internally consistent, CORRECT. They are deliberately untouched. This is
    the W1/[C3] heartbeat lesson exactly: the value looks like the bug class, every consumer agrees
    with every other, and "fixing" one side is what would break it.

[4] THE BULK REWRITE OVERREACHED, AND IT WAS CAUGHT. The regex rewrote 51 sites, not 49 — two in

## 2026-09-17 - W30 EXECUTED — R26 F3, the W22 cached-snapshot class (six findings, one seam)

Plan: `Plans4agent_next_session/W30_plan_R26_F3_w22_cache_class.md`, archived verbatim at
`reports/w30_plan_20260917.md`. All six findings landed together (they share one seam and the
plan's own decision was to keep R26's F3 grouping intact).

**The seam.** `PositionReconciler.reconcile()` built `ibkr_map` from `get_positions()` — the CACHE,
which reads back EMPTY on any disconnect/Gateway hiccup exactly like a genuinely flat book
(`get_positions_fresh`'s own docstring). Two call sites acted on that cache as if it were
authoritative: the `HALT_UNTRACKED` clear (`elif _halt_path.exists(): unlink()`) and
`reconcile_declared_positions()` (four `delete_state` calls + a "closed" Telegram message). FIX:
when `ibkr_positions` (the raw cache read) is empty, resolve via `get_positions_fresh()` once —
`None` (broker won't answer) skips BOTH the unlink and the declared-position cleanup for this pass
and logs `declared_position_reconcile_unconfirmed`; a real (possibly empty) fresh list authorizes
both, keyed via the existing `_fresh_leg_keys()` (same key shape as `ibkr_map`, no mismatch trap).
A client exposing no `get_positions_fresh` at all (legacy/test double) falls back to the pre-W30
cache-trusting behaviour rather than wedging the freeze/cleanup open forever — this is what keeps
every existing `test_w22_*` test green with zero changes to those files: none of them attach a
`get_positions_fresh` mock, so none of them exercise the new gate; it only activates when the
client actually supports the authoritative query, which the real `IBKRClient` always does.

**#3 [design].** A declared manual position has no local trade row, so
`orchestrator._sync_risk_manager_positions` (the sole producer of `RiskManager._open_positions`)
never saw it — invisible to the aggregate capital-at-risk cap, symbol concentration, per-expiry
cap, correlation, and the open-position count. Fixed via new
`PositionReconciler.declared_position_risk_rows()`: one synthesized row per declared key from the
broker's own cached position, priced through `RiskManager._structural_max_loss` (naked-short Reg-T
proxy) with an `avgCost`-based floor for the long-option case; wired into
`_sync_risk_manager_positions` right before `update_positions()`. The false claim in
`manual_positions.py`'s own module docstring ("exposure already counted via `ib.portfolio()`") is
corrected in place — true for `portfolio.py`'s exposure/delta/mark functions, never true for the
risk manager.

**#4 (never-answered keys leak).** `reconcile_declared_positions()` only ever swept keys with a
recorded "yes" answer. A key that was sighted/confirmed/prompted but never answered, then vanished
from the broker, leaked its `last_seen`/`confirmed`/`msgid` rows forever — a LATER, genuinely new
sighting of the identical contract then skipped the R5 debounce entirely (stale `confirmed` flag)
and never re-prompted (stale `msgid` read as "already asked"). Fixed with a second sweep pass over
`_LAST_SEEN_PREFIX` keys with no recorded answer, and a shared `_clear_key_state()` helper (one
place that knows every prefix this module writes, so a cleanup path can no longer miss one). "no"-
answered keys are deliberately left untouched, unchanged from before.

**#5 (declared key is contract identity only).** `is_declared()` matched on
`symbol:strike:right:expiry` alone, no quantity — a later, undeclared size increase on an already-
approved contract (declare −1, broker later shows −3) went unnoticed by every risk gate. New
`manual_positions.declared_quantity_matches()` compares the CURRENT broker quantity against the
quantity recorded at prompt time (`prompt_if_needed` now stamps `manual_position_declared_qty_
<key>`); a mismatch clears only the answer/msgid/qty (deliberately NOT the sighting/confirmed
state), so the size change freezes and re-prompts on the SAME pass rather than waiting through a
fresh 2-sighting debounce — a size change on an approved contract is MORE suspect than a brand-new
untracked one, not less. A key declared before this quantity tracking existed (no recorded qty) is
grandfathered as a match rather than auto-frozen on deploy — preserves every pre-existing
`test_w22_*` fixture and any live declared position with no baseline to compare against.

**#6 (`reconcile_now()` discards its result).** Restored the same `closing_exit_orders` →
`executor.adopt_exit_order()` re-adoption the startup and post-market call sites already do — a
kept-CLOSING trade's working exit order answered via Telegram used to come back invisible. Added a
connection guard (`if not self._ibkr.connected: return`) — `reconcile_now` runs DETACHED from a
Telegram reply at ANY time, including mid-shutdown after IBKR disconnects. Added
`manual_positions.drain_background_tasks()` (bounded `asyncio.wait` over the module's own
`_background_tasks` set) and wired it into `main.py`'s shutdown, between the poller cancellation
and `ibkr.disconnect()` — an answer recorded right as the bot shuts down no longer risks its

## 2026-09-17 - LIVE INCIDENT FIXED: the market_data watchdog false alarm

Not a register finding, not part of R26 or any numbered wave — a live-ops bug the operator flagged
mid-session ("WATCHDOG ALERT: market_data is DOWN and recovery failed... since 3:58pm"), traced and
fixed end to end in this entry.

[1] THE INVESTIGATION, because the wrong diagnosis was very nearly the reported one. The alert
    text matched `watchdog.py:282` exactly, so the mechanism was never in doubt — but the FIRST
    hypothesis (an active market-data outage, motivated by the sheer volume of live Error 10091 /
    "Unknown contract" noise for SPY/IWM options in `logs/bot_stdout.log`) was wrong, and ruled out
    by evidence rather than assumption:
      - Error 10091 is NOT new: a comment already sitting in `options_chain.py`
        ("R16... confirmed live 2026-09-14... confirmed benign for reqMktData... not a symptom to
        chase here") shows a prior audit round investigated this EXACT noise on this EXACT code
        path and closed it as harmless. Re-reading old comments before chasing new alarms would
        have saved a detour.
      - "Unknown contract" is ib_insync's own internal wording (confirmed: zero hits for that
        string anywhere in `src/`), and the code that triggers it (`qualifyContractsAsync` inside
        `_fetch_ibkr_expiry`) already filters failed qualifications out (`conId != 0`) — a normal,
        tolerated consequence of `reqSecDefOptParams` returning a strikes UNION across expiries,
        not a fetch failure.
      - `hist_data_error` / `hist_data_empty` (the actual gate in front of the `market_data`
        heartbeat): ZERO occurrences today. The underlying daily-bar fetch was never failing.
      - Polygon auth failures (an R26-noted, genuinely-live operator item): ZERO occurrences today.
    THE REAL EVIDENCE: `ml_prediction` log events (fired unconditionally two lines after the
    heartbeat, in the same execution path) at 18:03:43, 18:07:15, 18:14:29, 18:17:50, 18:21:23,
    18:28:32 UTC — the last one 90 SECONDS before this was checked. The scan loop was running,
    successfully, continuously, in real time. Gaps between consecutive events: 213s, 434s, 201s,
    213s, 429s — **every single one exceeding the 120-second timeout**.

[2] ROOT CAUSE. `Watchdog()` at `orchestrator.py` uses the class default `heartbeat_timeout=120.0`
    for EVERY registered component, uniformly — there was no per-component override anywhere in
    the class. `market_data` heartbeats exactly once per SYMBOL inside a FULL scan cycle
    (`scan_interval_seconds`, 300s), never on the 30s fast-loop tick that keeps `trading_loop` and
    `ibkr` fresh against that same 120s window. The natural gap between market_data heartbeats was
    therefore ALWAYS going to exceed 120s, on every single cycle, by architecture — not by fault.
    Compounding it: `market_data` has NO recovery callback registered (only `ibkr` does, via
    `on_recovery("ibkr", self._ibkr.ensure_connected)`). `check_and_recover()`'s alert branch fires
    UNCONDITIONALLY whenever a component is found DOWN and nothing recovered it — so this was
    guaranteed to repage on every ~5-minute `check_and_recover` tick, indefinitely, exactly matching
    "getting these messages... since 3:58pm."

[3] THE FIX. `ComponentHealth` gains an optional `heartbeat_timeout: float | None` field (None =
    fall back to the instance default — existing single-timeout behaviour, unchanged, when unset).
    `register_component(name, *, heartbeat_timeout=None)` — keyword-only, so every existing
    single-argument call site (`register_component("trading_loop")`, `("ibkr")`, three more in
    `tests/test_w6_ops_surfaces.py`, five in `tests/test_watchdog.py` itself) is untouched;
    confirmed by grep before changing the signature. `_compute_health()`'s staleness check now
    reads the per-component override when set.
    `orchestrator.py` registers `market_data` with `heartbeat_timeout=3 * scan_interval_seconds`
    (900s) — derived from the live config value rather than a new hardcoded literal, sized with
    real margin: 900s comfortably covers the measured worst gap (434s, ~1.4x one cycle) while still
    paging within 2-3 missed cycles of a genuine stall.

[4] PROVEN, NOT ASSUMED, in both directions.
      - Ran the fix against the REAL measured worst-case gap (434s): `market_data` stays HEALTHY;
        `trading_loop`, unaffected by the change (no override requested for it), correctly still
        reads DOWN at that same 434s gap — proving the fix is scoped to the one component that
        needed it, not a blanket loosening.
      - Ran it against 1000s (beyond the 900s override): still correctly DOWN — guards against
        over-correcting into a monitor that never alerts.
      - NEGATIVE CONTROL, disabled and confirmed: forced the staleness check back onto the shared
        instance timeout only (simulating the pre-fix single-timeout shape) and re-ran the new test
        class. Exactly the three tests asserting the override actually works FAILED — including an
        end-to-end one that fires the real alert text
        (`"ALERT: market_data is DOWN and recovery failed..."`) through the real `check_and_recover`
        path. The other five (negative control itself, the genuine-stall guard, backward-compat,
        auto-registration) correctly stayed green, since they do not depend on the override at all.
        Restored immediately after; all 20 tests in the file green again.

[5] VERIFICATION. `tests/test_watchdog.py`, 8 new tests (12 -> 20). Full fast lane
    **1936 passed / 45 skipped / 1 failed** (the known local-`.env` `test_r19_config_authority`
    case) — zero new or unexpected failures. Notably, the PRIOR run's `test_watchdog.py::
    TestOverallHealth` flakiness (diagnosed in the W30 entry above as a too-tight 5.0s test-fixture
    margin tripping under system load) did NOT recur here, one more data point for that diagnosis
    being load-related rather than a real defect. `compileall` OK, `scripts/typecheck.py` OK,
    `scripts/smoke_deploy.py` -> SMOKE PASS (13 checks). Orchestrator-adjacent files re-run given
    `__init__` was touched: `test_w2_orchestrator_gates.py` + `test_w6_ops_surfaces.py` +
    `test_hot_path_smoke.py`, 114 passed.

STATE AT HANDOFF: **DEPLOYED nowhere yet — staged, like W28/W29/W30.** `watchdog.py` and

## 2026-09-18 - W32 EXECUTED — R26 F2, booking & breaker integrity (three findings, one seam)

NUMBERING: W31 stays reserved for Ahmed's queued R26 F4 (the W25 sizing self-test). The Windows box
takes **W32-W35** for the fix sets assigned to it in `reports/r26_integration_20260917.md`:
W32 = F2 (this entry), W33 = F1 (exit rebuild corrective), W34 = F6 (ops substrate),
W35 = F8 + the F7 share. Ahmed's queue continues at W31 and then W36+.

WHAT R26 FOUND (all three reproduced against the tree before anything was changed):

[1] two-phase-claim-double-books (live_money). W14 made the outbox claim a MARK instead of a
    delete, which fixed the lost-close half of the race and left the double-book half open: the
    booking body was five independent writes (daily_stats, breaker, PDT, Thompson, drift) with the
    outbox row deleted last. A lock, a crash, or an exception after the first write left the row in
    place, and the drain re-booked the WHOLE close on its next pass — the P&L added to daily_stats
    twice and the loss counted twice against the breaker's streak. Reproduced with a store that
    fails once after the stats write: total_pnl -200 for a single -100 close, consecutive_losses 2.

[2] breaker-unreadable-never-reloads (live_money, fail-open). W14 stopped a breaker that could not
    read its store from OVERWRITING the intact blob with zeros. Nothing ever read the blob again.
    One transient `database is locked` at startup left the breaker on a zero placeholder for the
    rest of the process: `is_tripped` lifted the fail-closed pause after one window without looking,
    persistence stayed off, and a daily-loss halt sitting intact on disk was not enforced.
    Reproduced: persisted tripped blob + one failing read -> `is_tripped` False 31 minutes later.

[3] concurrency-03 residual (live_money). W14 taught the FILL path that a refused CAS can mean
    "the sweep promoted this row to FILLED first" rather than "terminal". Its twin,
    `_update_trade_partial`, kept the old reading: the real partial quantity was discarded, the row
    stayed FILLED at the full SIGNAL size (so the reverse-combo exit was sized larger than the live
    position) and a false CRITICAL page fired. Separately the page flag was ONE key
    (`alert_fill_after_close`), so a second refusal overwrote the first and only the last was paged.

WHAT CHANGED:

  - `state.py`: `exit_outbox` gains `core_booked` and `steps_done`. `book_exit_core()` lands
    daily_stats, the breaker blob and the `core_booked` marker in ONE `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction;
    a second call for the same close is a no-op that returns False. `mark_exit_step()` /
    `exit_steps_done()` record each non-money side effect so a retry skips what already landed.
  - `circuit_breaker.py`: `snapshot()`/`restore()`/`persistable_blob()` so the orchestrator can apply
    a result in memory, write it inside the state transaction, and undo it if that transaction
    fails. `_maybe_reload()` re-reads the store at most every 30s while unreadable; `is_tripped`
    returns True until a read succeeds; results recorded while blind are queued and replayed onto
    the store's truth once it does.
  - `orchestrator.py`: both booking paths (`_process_completed_exits`, `_drain_exit_outbox`) go
    through `_book_exit_core` then the flagged steps pdt/thompson/drift/notify; the outbox row is
    completed only when every step has landed. A core failure in the callback path is deferred to
    the drain rather than half-booked. The fill-after-close pager drains every
    `alert_fill_after_close_<trade_id>` key (and the bare pre-W32 key if one is still stored).
  - `executor.py`: `_update_trade_partial` reads the actual status on a refused CAS — terminal rows
    bail and flag per trade; a promoted FILLED row gets the REAL partial quantity and price.

PROOF. `tests/test_w32_booking_breaker_integrity.py`, 16 executing tests. Re-run against the
pre-fix source in this session (the four `src/` files stashed, tests kept): **14 failed, 2 passed**.
The two green ones are the controls that must hold on both trees —
`test_re_reads_are_rate_limited` and `test_a_terminal_row_is_still_refused`. No `inspect.getsource`. Three existing tests asserted the old seam and were moved
to the new one with the same intent (`test_w1`, `test_w14` per-trade key; `test_r15` now asserts
`book_exit_core` receives the trued-up P&L). W14's `test_the_intact_streak_survives_a_locked_relaunch`
was the F7 "cannot fail" case — its mock swallowed the write it claimed to guard. Rebuilt on a
wrapper whose reads fail and whose writes reach the real store, and proven RED with the W14 latch
removed.

VERIFICATION (Windows box, the live host): full fast lane **1952 passed / 46 skipped / 0 failed**
(490s); `scripts/typecheck.py` OK.

STATE AT HANDOFF: committed and pushed, **deployed nowhere**. The running bot (PID 16684) is on
c368a0f with one QQQ condor open; `state.py`, `orchestrator.py`, `executor.py` and
`circuit_breaker.py` are all loaded by it, so W32 takes effect at the next restart. The
`exit_outbox` migration is additive (two defaulted columns) and runs at StateManager init.

## 2026-09-18 - W33 EXECUTED — R26 F1, the W7 exit rebuild corrected (seven findings + two riders)

WHY THIS ONE FIRST AFTER F2: a QQQ condor is open (T-20260917-095601-aa4fa8, +16% at 11:50 ET, 40%
take-profit tier). Its exit will run this code path. On 09-11 that path produced seven consecutive
band-rejected orders in sixteen minutes and only cleared when the BAG happened to quote.

W7 shipped 20/20 green with every one of these defects present, because each W7 test called one
helper in isolation with a fresh mark in hand. Every W33 test drives the real path instead: the real
ib_insync `Wrapper`, the real `IBKRClient`, the real `TradeExecutor.check_fills`, the real
`_close_multi_leg`.

THE SEVEN, AND WHAT CHANGED:

[1] exit-band-reject-text-never-reaches-parser. ib_insync 0.9.86 lists 202 in `warningCodes` and
    never appends a warning to `trade.log` (pinned by a test, so an upgrade that changes this is
    noticed). `ib.errorEvent` was the only route and nothing subscribed. No `exit_band_*` key has
    ever been written — 204 `Warning 202` lines in the retained logs, zero captures — so every band
    rule W7 built was inert. `IBKRClient` now subscribes, keeps the broker's text per orderId for
    codes 110/201/202/10318 (bounded: 256 orders x 8 messages), and `check_fills` reads it next to
    the order log. Proven wire-to-state: `Wrapper.error(77, 202, <the verbatim 09-11 text>)` +
    `orderStatus(Cancelled)` -> `bot_state['exit_band_T-SPY'] == {band: 3.69, market: 3.17}`.

[2] band-cap-clamps-at-or-above-the-band. `max(min(l, b), min(f, b))` with `l > b` is `b` on every
    input, and IBKR's text is "at or MORE aggressive than". `_under_band()` lands one whole tick
    below (1.745 -> 1.74, 3.50 -> 3.49); a mark-derived floor can no longer lift it back over.

[3] no-quote-fallback-prices-at-the-ceiling. The ceiling WAS the order price: 1.5 x mark, 0.94-1.14
    above the stated band on 7 of 7 live attempts, identical on every backoff. A no-quote order is
    now `anchor + cross + n * exit_reprice_step`, capped — the ceiling is only ever a cap. `n`
    counts this trade's consecutive no-quote placements (own counter: R14's strike count resets on
    the slow re-price cadence, which is exactly the resting-unfilled case that needs the step). All
    seven live 09-11 marks now price under their own bands on the first attempt (3.29 vs 3.69).

[4] zero-bid-sold-wing-aborts-leg-synthesis and [5] one-sided-leg-priced-from-the-wrong-side. Every
    leg is priced from its conservative side and never the other: a leg we buy needs an OFFER (bid
    only -> None, a decision rather than an accident); a leg we sell is worth its bid, and 0.00 is a
    bid. IBKR's -1 ("nobody bids") contributes 0 on a CREDIT buyback only. That restriction is not
    in the audit's suggested fix and is deliberate: the first version applied it everywhere and the
    R13 suite caught it pricing a long straddle's close at zero — giving the position away. NaN / a
    silent ticker is missing data, not a quote, and still returns None, so a dead feed cannot
    synthesize a price from half the legs.

[6] mark-ceiling-clamps-below-the-ask-at-low-marks. The ceiling is compared with an ask-side price
    while the mark is a mid, and a four-leg half-spread does not shrink with the mark (0.52-0.58
    measured on QQQ 09-11). `exit_min_ceiling_headroom` (0.60) floors the headroom:
    `mark + max(cross, (mult-1)*mark, headroom)`. The probe case (mark 0.60, legs offering 1.08) now
    places 1.18, was 0.90. The incident ceilings are unchanged (1.40 -> 2.10, 8.76 -> 13.14) and the
    R13 garbage-quote guard still binds (9.90 ask on a 1.00 mark -> 1.60).

[7] raw-wing-width-fallback-still-reachable. A mark 901s old priced the exit at the raw width
    ($39-60 wings: the structural max loss; 0.90 vs 39.00 for a 120-second difference in mark age).
    Now: a stale mark is still the anchor (cap widened to the blind cap, since the market may have
    moved); with no mark at all the anchor is the entry credit; the blind cap is
    `min(width, exit_blind_credit_multiple * credit)` (2.0). With nothing to anchor on, refuse and
    page. DEVIATION FROM THE AUDIT'S SUGGESTION: it asked for `entry_credit + k * expected_move`.
    Expected move needs spot and IV, which are unavailable in exactly the no-feed state this branch
    handles; the entry credit is the one number always in hand.

RIDERS: `stale-exit-quality-tuple` (F8) — `_last_exit_quality` is cleared at the top of every
multi-leg close and set by the no-quote branch, so a non-placing exit can no longer hand its numbers
to the next trade's slippage record. Poll telemetry — one `combo_exit_quote_poll` line per attempt
with what the BAG and each leg actually showed (`nan/nan`, `0/nan`, `-1/0.05`); the 09-11 diagnosis
had to be reconstructed from a probe because nothing logged it.

A HAZARD W33 CREATES AND CLOSES. Bands were never captured before, so W7's one-hour band lifetime
was never exercised. Live, it would cap a touch stop at 13:50 below a market that had moved through
a band stated against a take-profit at 13:31 — and an order under the market draws no new reject to
correct it. Bands now expire after `exit_band_ttl_seconds` (300; a live reject loop re-states one
every 30-180s) and are ignored once the fresh mark has risen to or through them.

TWO R13 TESTS CHANGED ON PURPOSE. `test_exit_order_safety.py` pinned "no quote -> LMT AT the width".
That is the finding. They now assert: still a LMT, still bounded by the width, still paged, priced

## 2026-09-18 - W35 EXECUTED — R26 F8 (research validity + config homes), the F7 share, and the deploy-order hazard closed

[1] THE TWO FINDINGS THAT REACH STRIKE SELECTION (`data/options_chain.py::_calculate_greeks`).
    On this feed contracts arrive with `implied_vol=0` and each one's IV is solved from its own
    quote. Everything chain-level was computed BEFORE that solve:
      - `iv_is_guessed` came from the pre-solve IV set, so a chain whose every contract solved
        cleanly from real prices was still flagged a guess — and `iron_condor.py` refuses a
        flagged chain (`degraded_greeks`).
      - `atm_iv` / `expected_move` are set in `OptionsChain.__post_init__` and were never
        refreshed: wings were sized from `atm_iv=0.0` -> the flat 0.20 fallback, and the
        expected-move gate saw 0, while the contracts carried a correct solved sigma.
      - the fallback sigma for a quote-less contract was the pre-solve median — i.e. the flat
        0.30 guess, in a chain whose other contracts solve to their real vol a few lines later.
    Now two passes: SOLVE every contract that can be; derive the median, the flag and (when
    anything was solved) `atm_iv`/`expected_move` from the post-solve set — read between the
    passes, so a backfilled sigma never counts as an observation; THEN backfill and compute
    Greeks. Tests generate quotes with py_vollib at a known sigma, so the answers are exact
    (six contracts at 0.22 -> atm_iv 0.22, EM = S*0.22*sqrt(30/365)).
    Two W19 tests pinned the defect: their "no usable IV anywhere" chain carried a solvable
    1.0 x 1.2 quote (the log shows attempted=2 contracts=2). They now use genuinely quote-less
    contracts, which is what the W19 gate is for.
    RESEARCH-VALIDITY NOTE: this changes what the live condor builder sees on every scan of the
    delayed-data path — real ATM vol instead of 0.20 for wing sizing, and no more spurious
    `degraded_greeks` refusals. Expect `atm_iv` in `condor_entry_quality` telemetry to become
    non-zero and entry counts to be able to rise. It starts at the next restart; it is a change
    to entry selection, so the verdict sample's entries from that restart onward are not
    like-for-like with those before it.

[2] range.pkl FLAPPED DAILY BETWEEN TWO SPECS. The live bot builds its range model from
    `ait.ml.range_spec.live_range_spec` (0.05, horizon 9 = the reachable hold). The supervisor's
    07:30 retrain script hardcoded `RangePredictor(threshold_pct=0.05, horizon_days=30)`, so every
    retrain rebuilt the artifact at a spec the live 0.65 floor was never calibrated for. (This
    corrects my own earlier wrong diagnosis of this symptom as a `horizon_days=None` key.) The
    script now reads the one authority. The test captures the script `retrain_models()` REALLY
    launches and executes it with training and I/O stubbed: pre-fix it built (0.05, 30).

[3] THE DEPLOY-ORDER HAZARD (registered in W33) IS CLOSED AT THE ROOT. `freeze_settings()`:
    the two long-lived entry points (`ait.main.run_bot`, the supervisor's `main()`) freeze the
    settings they started with; every later `load_settings()` in that process returns a COPY of
    that snapshot and never re-reads the file. Proven with real processes: load, then add an
    unknown key to config.yaml, then reload -> `ValidationError` without the freeze (the control —

    NOT YET LIVE: the processes started at 12:20 predate this. Until the next restart, adding a

## 2026-09-20 - W38 EXECUTED — R26 F5: the W21 convention change's unmigrated readers

First of three waves clearing this box's remaining R26 queue (W38 = F5 remainder, W39 = the two
W22 Telegram rows, W40 = the F7 rows outside `test_w25_sizing_coherence.py`). Sequential, not
batched, because the blast radii differ: this one changes what the dashboard and the Friday
scorecard REPORT.

THE SHAPE OF F5, because it is not what the fix-set line suggests. W21 enumerated its readers by
grepping `fromisoformat` and walking its AST. That method is blind to two whole classes — SQL date
functions, and a function that calls a HELPER naming a migrated column — and R26 found three
survivors in exactly those blind spots. The script half is separate and was done first because it
gates the Windows box's migration.

[1] `--apply` IS A NO-OP ON THIS BOX, AND THE LEDGER SHOULD SAY SO. R26 F5 #1 reads "run
    `scripts/restate_w21_tz_aware.py --apply` with the bot stopped". Measured here read-only:
    **12/12 trades carry an offset on both columns, 0 naive values across all five target
    columns**, and the pre-migration snapshot `data/backups/ait_state.pre_w21_tz.20260916_133646.db`
    exists locally holding the naive pre-state. R26's "0 of 30 live rows are tz-aware" was measured
    on the WINDOWS box (its §-header records the bot running with pids this DB has never seen).
    Running it here takes the `nothing to do` return, which PRECEDES the snapshot — so it writes
    nothing, snapshots nothing, and proves nothing. A LEDGER CORRECTION while I am here:
    PLAN.md:3405's "10 trades, ALL entered 2026-04-23/24" describes neither box today (this one has
    12 trades, two of them 2026-09-17). The migration is handed to the Windows box as a RUNBOOK
    step with independent verification — see [6].

[2] THE POST-CONDITION COULD NOT FAIL (R26 `w21-restate-post-condition-is-unsatisfiable`). The
    script's own verification read `parse_trade_ts(row[col]).tzinfo is None`, and `parse_trade_ts`
    localises naive input and converts aware input — it can NEVER return naive. So `bad` stayed 0,
    the success line always printed, and `main()` returned 0 even for a run that wrote nothing: the
    one automated statement an operator would rely on to confirm the money-bearing corpus really
    migrated was a constant. Now reads the STORED text via `fromisoformat`, with an unparseable row
    reported as `POST-CHECK UNPARSEABLE` rather than raising AFTER the writes.
    REPRODUCED, then closed: against a pre-W38 copy with a trigger reverting every UPDATE, the
    script printed `post-check: every stored timestamp is timezone-aware` and returned **0** with
    the row still naive. Post-fix the same scenario returns 1.

[3] THE SCRIPT HAD ZERO TEST COVERAGE (R26 `w21-restate-script-has-zero-test-coverage`) — nothing
    executed `main()`; the only `restate_w21` string in `tests/` was an assertion MESSAGE. `main()`
    gains `argv` / `db_path` / `host_move` seams (defaults reproduce the command line exactly, so
    `__main__` and every operator invocation are unchanged), and 14 tests now drive it against
    throwaway DBs. The highest-value one is the **HOST_MOVE abort**: a plain string compare against
    `"2026-09-14"` that is the only thing standing between a convention change and a silent
    restatement of the trading record, and it had never been executed. Also pinned: idempotency,
    the snapshot holding the PRE state, per-row EST/EDT derivation (-05:00 in January, -04:00 in
    July), that an abort leaves the DB BYTE-IDENTICAL, and that the "nothing to do" path takes no
    snapshot — [1]'s behaviour, so it cannot be mistaken for a backup.
    Also corrected: the docstring pointed at a `--before` flag that does not exist and never did.

[4] THE DASHBOARD BUCKETED BY THE UTC DAY (R26 `w21-sqlite-date-normalises-aware-timestamps-to-utc`).
    SQLite's date functions convert an offset-bearing ISO string to UTC first and leave a naive one
    alone, so W21's aware writes silently changed what seven queries MEAN:
        date('2026-09-13T21:05:00')       -> '2026-09-13'   the ET day
        date('2026-09-13T21:05:00-04:00') -> '2026-09-14'   the UTC day
        strftime('%w', ...)               -> '0' vs '1'     Sunday vs Monday
    Any close at or after 20:00 EDT landed in tomorrow's P&L row, tomorrow's calendar cell and
    tomorrow's weekday bucket, while `master.py`'s LIKE counters and every `parse_trade_ts` caller
    still called it today — two irreconcilable daily series over one table, nothing raised. **This
    is LIVE on this box, not latent**: every row here is now aware.
    Six sites take `substr(COALESCE(exit_time, entry_time),1,10)`; the seventh is different and the
    plan initially got it wrong — `strftime('%w', entry_time)` needs `strftime` OVER `substr`,
    because substr alone yields no weekday. Declared as `_ET_DAY_WINDOW_SQL` /
    `_ET_ENTRY_WEEKDAY_SQL` beside the existing `_REAL_CLOSE_SQL`, so the tests bind the same text
    the app runs rather than reading source.
    CLASS GUARD, which is the payoff: a scan for `date(`/`strftime(`/`julianday(`/`datetime(`
    applied directly to a migrated column — the check W21's `fromisoformat` walk structurally could
    not make. Run against the PRE-FIX file it reports exactly **7 offenders**, matching the 7 sites
    fixed; against HEAD, zero.

[5] `_mirror_lag` WAS AN UNMIGRATED READER (R26 `w21-mirror-lag-is-an-unmigrated-reader`). Bare
    `fromisoformat` on both sides, so a naive/aware pair raised TypeError into a bare `except` and
    the digest degraded from "mirror BEHIND live by 28h" to a bare "BEHIND" with no magnitude —
    exactly when the mirror IS behind, leaving the operator unable to tell a one-run lag from the
    multi-day 07-14 failure the check exists to catch. W21's function-scoped guard could not see it
    because the function's own body never names a migrated column; they live in `_newest_trade_ts`.

## 2026-09-20 - W39 EXECUTED — R26 F6 rows 7-8: the Telegram poller stops dropping updates in silence

Second of the three waves clearing this box's R26 queue. These two rows are in
`execution/manual_positions.py` — this box's module — and were explicitly skipped by the other
box's W34 (PLAN.md:5694-5697) for that reason.

ONE OF THE TWO FINDINGS WAS ALREADY CLOSED, AND SAYING SO IS THE POINT OF THIS ENTRY. The wave
plan named both as fixes. Re-deriving them at HEAD first — the programme's own rule, that a
finding closes when its reproduction stops reproducing — showed one of them already does not
reproduce. It is recorded as closed BY W30, not by this wave.

[1] FINDING A, `w22-unrecognised-telegram-updates-are-dropped-with-no-trace` — REAL, FIXED.
    Four drop paths in `_handle_update` emitted nothing at all. Reproduced against a pre-fix copy
    of the module before anything changed:
        PRE-FIX 'yes please'      -> replies=[]  discard_logs=[]
        PRE-FIX callback, no msg  -> answered=[]     (the button spins forever)
        PRE-FIX foreign callback  -> answered=[]
    The sharpest is the text path. The prompt invites a free-form reply; the parser accepts exactly
    four tokens and discarded everything else with no edit, no confirmation and no log — while
    `HALT_UNTRACKED` kept every new entry frozen. "The answer never came" was undiagnosable:
    identical in the logs to a prompt never seen, a `getUpdates` outage, or a dead poller.
    All four now log `manual_position_update_discarded` with a reason. Both callback paths
    `answer_callback()` BEFORE returning — an unanswered callback_query leaves the button spinning
    on the operator's phone, and answering is a transport obligation, not an endorsement of the
    tap. `cq.get("message") or {}` made an ABSENT message behave exactly like a foreign-chat one,
    so both fell through having answered nothing; they are separate branches now.
    Unrecognised text in the CONFIGURED chat gets a reply naming the accepted tokens, throttled to
    one nudge per five minutes so a chatty chat cannot turn the poller into an echo loop, and only
    when something is actually pending. A foreign chat is logged and never replied to — answering
    would leak the bot's existence to it. `_ACCEPTED_REPLIES` is declared once and interpolated
    into both prompts, so the guidance the operator is shown cannot drift from what the parser
    takes; that drift IS the finding.

[2] FINDING B, `w22-leaked-msgid-keeps-a-dead-position-pending-forever` — **CLOSED BY W30.**
    Measured at HEAD with a real StateManager, both halves the finding names:
        prompted, unanswered      -> pending_keys ['QQQ:712.0:C:2026-09-18']   digest {…}
        after authoritative sweep -> pending_keys []                            digest set()
    A `manual_position_prompt_msgid_` row can only exist downstream of `record_sighting()`, so a
    `manual_position_last_seen_` row always accompanies it, and W30's second cleanup loop
    (`manual_positions.py:418-425`) clears both through `_clear_key_state`. The finding treats
    `pending_keys()` and the digest's `awaiting_reply` as two separate leaks; they read the SAME
    msgid row, so both self-heal on the next pass that can confirm the broker set.
    AND R26's SUGGESTED FIX IS NOT IMPLEMENTABLE AS WRITTEN — "filter to keys still present at the
    broker". The only state in which a stale prompt lingers is the one where the sweep is SKIPPED
    because the broker set is not authoritative, so there is nothing authoritative to filter
    against; and the digest runs in the SUPERVISOR, which has no IB connection at all. The obvious
    proxy is worse than nothing: a `last_seen` freshness TTL would mark a genuinely live position
    stale every morning, because no reconcile passes run overnight. Inferring presence there is
    precisely the guessing W30 removed when it made this path fail closed.
    SO THE RESIDUAL IS TREATED AS WHAT IT IS: a correct fail-closed skip that was INVISIBLE. The
    skip now logs `manual_position_cleanup_skipped` with its reason and the pending count, because
    that window is the only one in which the operator can see "awaiting your reply" for a position
    that is long gone, and nothing explained why. Three regression tests pin the self-healing so a
    future change to the sweep cannot silently reopen the finding, with a control that a position
    still AT the broker keeps its prompt.

[3] THE CONFIG SWITCH SWITCHED NOTHING. `notifications.telegram.enabled`, plus `send_trades`,
    `send_errors`, `send_daily_summary` and `send_circuit_breaker`, were declared in `config.yaml`
    and in `TelegramConfig` and read by NOTHING in `src/` — the only real switch was whether `.env`
    carried a token and a chat id. An operator setting `enabled: false` to silence a misbehaving
    poller changed nothing at all. Same R19c dead-config class W36 fixed for ten trading knobs,
    with a safety edge: this is the switch someone reaches for in a hurry.
    `enabled` is now wired at the single construction site (`main.py`), as
    `configured and enabled`, and a disabled notifier logs `telegram_disabled_by_config` naming the
    consequence — the manual-position POLLER skips when the notifier is disabled, so
    `HALT_UNTRACKED` prompts can no longer be answered and entries stay frozen. That is not
    obvious from the knob's name, so it is in the warning, the field description and the yaml.
    THE OTHER FOUR WERE DELETED, NOT WIRED. Gating `_alert` / `_send_notification` /
    `send_circuit_breaker_alert` on four config booleans would add four new FAIL-OPEN decisions on
    alert paths — an alert that silently does not fire is the R8 class this programme keeps
    fixing. Per-category muting, if it is ever wanted, needs its own wave with a test per path.
    `extra="forbid"` means the model and the yaml had to land in the same commit.

[4] ONE EXISTING TEST INVERTED, and it pinned the defect exactly.
    `test_callback_from_a_different_chat_is_ignored` asserted `tg.answered_callbacks == []` — i.e.
    it required the spinning button. Its INTENT (never act on a foreign chat's input) is unchanged
    and still asserted, now joined by "and never reply into it" and the discard log line. Also
    strengthened: `test_reply_to_an_unmatched_message_id_is_ignored_not_misapplied` still proves
    the reply is not guessed at, and now also proves the operator is told.
    A TEST-INFRASTRUCTURE NOTE worth carrying forward: `caplog` sees NOTHING from this project's
    logging. structlog does not route through stdlib handlers, so the first version of these
    assertions passed vacuously against lines that were being emitted to stdout the whole time.
    The `discards` fixture records the real module logger instead. An autouse fixture also resets
    the module-level nudge throttle between tests — without it the first test to nudge silences
    every later one and the file depends on collection order.

PROOF. `tests/test_w39_telegram_visibility.py` (10) and 6 added to
`tests/test_w22_manual_positions.py` (34 -> 40). Finding A's pre-fix evidence is the transcript in
[1], taken against `HEAD:src/ait/execution/manual_positions.py` loaded as a separate module — the

Controls that must hold on both trees: a real four-token answer still records, a live position

## 2026-09-21 - W40 EXECUTED — R26 F7: the tests that could not fail, and four ledger retractions

Last of the three waves clearing this box's R26 queue. F7 is about TEST HONESTY: tests that claim
to prove something and cannot fail, and ledger claims resting on them. Almost no production code —
two small changes, both made because a TEST was constraining the source it was meant to observe.

THE RULE BEING APPLIED, which this project already wrote down and then broke in its own fixes
(PLAN.md:1138): *a source-string assertion proves code was WRITTEN, never that it RUNS — and it
decays into a silent no-op on rename.*

[1] W18's THROTTLE CLASS EXECUTED ONE OF THE FOUR SITES IT CLAIMED
    (`w18-throttle-tests-getsource-and-three-of-four-sites`). The class is named
    `TestThrottleOrderingCoversAllFourSites` and its docstring said "These tests pin all four".
    It executed ONE (`health_check`), pinned two with `inspect.getsource`, and left the fourth —
    in `BotManager.start()` — with no assertion coverage anywhere in the suite. R26 measured the
    cost: reverting `start()` to consume-on-drop left all 308 supervisor tests green, and the whole
    suite unchanged at 8 failed / 1841 passed.
    THE getsource PIN WAS WORSE THAN HOLLOW BY THE TIME W40 REACHED IT. It asserted
    `src.count("if _alert(") == 2` and that a whitespace-exact literal containing
    `self._last_gateway_alert = now` was absent from `_maybe_recover_gateway`. R26 showed it was
    already inert (adding `or True` to both gates left the class reporting 3 passed); then W34
    moved those two pages onto their own `_last_gateway_escalation` latch, so the method stopped
    containing the string `_last_gateway_alert` at all and the second assertion became
    UNCONDITIONALLY TRUE. Exactly the decay-on-rename the standing lesson names.
    All four sites are now driven through the real methods: two over `_maybe_recover_gateway`
    (dropped page must not burn the escalation latch; delivered page must still throttle) and two
    over `start()`. MUTATION PROOF for the site that had none — reverting `start()` to
    consume-on-drop, line-count preserving per PLAN.md:2569-2574 — gives **1 failed / 15 passed**,
    the failure being `test_the_start_site_retries_after_a_dropped_page`.
    A TRAP WORTH RECORDING: `ensure_gateway` is imported INSIDE `start()`, so patching
    `M.ensure_gateway` silently does nothing and the real launcher runs. The test patches
    `ait.orchestration.gateway.ensure_gateway`.

[2] THE TWO `read_text()` TESTS IN THE SAME FILE, rebuilt.
    The capital-literal one regexed three source files for `196000`; it could not observe whether
    any module EXECUTES a fallback, and a reintroduced literal spelled `196_000` or `1.96e5` passed
    it cleanly. It now MOVES the authority (`AIT_CAPITAL_BASE`) and requires every module's
    resolved base to move with it — a module carrying its own diverges whatever its spelling.
    The dashboard-key one substring-matched `key = 'last_net_liquidation'` in `app.py` and
    `set_state("last_net_liquidation"` in `orchestrator.py`. It had ALREADY broken once for no
    behavioural reason: W29 reformatted the `set_state` call across three lines and it went red
    (PLAN.md:5073-5084 registered it for this sweep). Worse, it had pushed a comment into
    PRODUCTION code — "KEEP THE set_state CALL ON ONE LINE" — so the test was constraining the
    source it was meant to observe. That comment is gone. The test now drives a REAL
    `_trading_cycle` through the hot-path smoke rig and reads the key back with the dashboard's OWN
    query, which is the round trip the contract always was. A rename on either side breaks it; a
    reformat cannot.
    PRODUCTION CHANGE, AND THE ONLY ONE IN THIS WAVE BESIDES THE DELETED COMMENT: the dashboard's
    account-value SQL is declared as `_NLV_QUERY` so the test binds the exact text the app runs —
    the same pattern W38 used for `_ET_DAY_WINDOW_SQL`, and the alternative to reading source.

[3] W22's BACKGROUND-TASK CLASS COULD NOT FAIL (`w22-background-task-test-cannot-fail`). Three
    assertions, none of which could go red:
      * `assert len(mp._background_tasks) >= 0` — true of every container, and asserted AFTER
        `asyncio.run()` had torn the loop down, when the set is empty either way.
      * `assert started == [True]` — holds whether or not a strong reference is kept, because
        `asyncio.run()` cancels-and-gathers pending tasks at shutdown and runs the coroutine to its
        first await regardless.
      * `assert len(...) == before` — SATISFIED BY THE DEFECT. The pre-fix implementation never
        added to the set, so before and after are both 0.
    The hazard is that the event loop holds only a WEAK reference, so an unreferenced task can be
    collected before it runs — observable only while the task is still PENDING, inside one running
    loop. Rebuilt that way: assert membership before awaiting, take a `weakref`, drop every local
    handle, `gc.collect()`, require the referent to survive, then release and require the set to
    return to 0 via the done-callback.
    MUTATION PROOF, using R26's own regression (`_fire_and_forget` reverted to a bare
    `asyncio.create_task(coro)`): **both rebuilt tests FAIL**, where the originals reported 2
    passed.

[4] LEDGER CORRECTIONS. Append-only, so these are corrections here and nothing above is edited.
    (a) **PLAN.md:2811 — RETRACTED.** "a new test pins all four so the class cannot regress again"
        is false, and was false when written. See [1]: one executed, two by source string, one
        uncovered. The W18 FIX itself was real and is not in question; the proof claim was not.
    (b) **PLAN.md:3921 — CORRECTED.** W22's "4 new tests" counts the class in [3] as evidence. Two

    (c) **PLAN.md:4396-4399 — DOWNGRADED from "confirmed" to "consistent with".** The W25 deploy

        from the live interpreter and read back inspect.getsource(...)"*. `inspect.getsource` reads
        the `.py` from DISK at import-time line offsets; it cannot distinguish code loaded into a
        running process from code edited onto disk a second earlier, so the cited evidence is
        equivalent to `cat src/ait/risk/manager.py` and is satisfied by any checkout at that HEAD.
        This project had already ruled on exactly that at PLAN.md:2571 and called it "the exact

        and W23 [5]), or a behaviour only the new code emits.

## 2026-09-21 - W41 EXECUTED — five cheap live-money floors, first wave of the unowned roadmap

First implementation wave of the 2026-09-21 roadmap entry above. No operator decision, no
re-probe — all five verified independently against HEAD before this wave started, and each
production defect reproduced against its pre-fix source before being fixed.

[1] `regress-live-05` — PDT history destroyed on an unreadable-store write. `pdt_guard.py`'s
    `_load_state()` already set `_state_unreadable=True` and failed closed on a bad READ
    (`can_day_trade()` blocks via `:159`); `_save_state()` wrote unconditionally, so the first
    `record_day_trade()` after a merely-TRANSIENT unreadable load persisted a fresh empty deque
    plus one entry OVER the real history. Reproduced against the untouched module first: a
    healthy guard persists 3 real entries; a guard whose store is wrapped to raise on every read
    (fakes only the failing verb, delegates the rest — the same idiom
    `test_w14_booking_exactly_once.py`'s intact-streak test uses) records one trade; the next
    fresh guard reads back **1 entry**, not 3.
    Fix: `record_day_trade` retries `_load_state()` when unreadable (the lock may already be gone
    by the time a trade closes) and, only while still unreadable, suppresses the persist and logs
    `pdt_history_write_suppressed_store_unverified` instead of writing.
    ONE ROUND OF SELF-CORRECTION WORTH RECORDING: the first cut retried-and-REPLACED — a second
    `record_day_trade` call landing exactly on the recovery boundary would silently drop the trade
    recorded during the outage from the persisted history (caught by my own test, not assumed
    safe). The finding's suggested fix names "re-read + merge", not "re-read" alone; the shipped
    version folds any not-yet-persisted in-memory entries back in after a successful re-load
    instead of overwriting them. Latent today only because `config.yaml:26
    pdt_account_under_25k: false`; it is the exact knob the sub-$25k funding plan flips.

[2] `time-authority-2` + `time-authority-4` — test-only. Verified directly against HEAD that both
    are already fixed: `executor.py:391` writes `entry_time=now_et().isoformat()` (W21, `c309d31`)
    and `orchestrator.py:3055` calls `would_hold_through_earnings(signal.symbol, today_et(),
    expiry_date)` (W28, `832f197`). Neither wave's own tests exercised these two call sites'
    ET-vs-host-clock behavior, which is what closes the finding.
    A DESIGN NOTE, because the first draft of these tests was wrong in an instructive way: the
    obvious approach — pin the process `TZ` env var (the `host_tz` fixture pattern used elsewhere
    in this project) and assert the code still reads ET — provides ZERO signal here. Verified by
    execution: `now_et()` is `datetime.now(ET)` with an explicit `tzinfo` argument, which is
    immune to the process `TZ` environment variable by construction (confirmed: identical output
    under `TZ=Europe/Berlin` and unset). The TZ trick only has power against a BARE
    `datetime.now()`/`date.today()` — exactly the class already retired at both sites. Testing
    already-fixed code with a tool built to catch the retired bug would have proven nothing; the
    shipped tests assert the real, host-independent structural properties instead (an AWARE ET
    offset on the entry-time write; a same-ET-day earnings block driven through the real
    `would_hold_through_earnings`).

[3] `model-vs-reality-margin-model-unimplemented`, piece 1 (of 2 — the deep half, `whatIfOrder` +
    `errorEvent` subscription, is W51). `can_afford` checked only `buying_power` (IBKR's ~4x
    leveraged figure); `available_funds` (cash after margin requirements) has always been fetched
    into every snapshot — same `accountSummary` subscription tuple as `buying_power`, confirmed at
    `account.py:237` — and was read by no gate anywhere. Reproduced pre-fix: `buying_power=$50,000,
    available_funds=$200` (a drained-margin account) approved a $1,000 trade. Fix:
    `min(snapshot.buying_power, snapshot.available_funds)`. Verified `available_funds` is not a
    key that can be legitimately absent while `buying_power` is present (identical fetch source),
    so no defensive fallback was added — an unconditional `min()` is correct, and a soft fallback
    would have been the R25 plat-06 class of defensive code masking a real depletion.

[4] `model-vs-reality-ex-div-assignment-void`, piece 1 (of 3 — the daily pre-ex-div check and the
    entry-blocking window are W51). The untracked-position loop in `reconciler.py` has three
    branches (OPT / STK / other); only OPT appended its key to `frozen_keys`, the list that becomes
    the `HALT_UNTRACKED` snapshot. The STK branch — the shape a short call's ASSIGNMENT leaves
    behind — logged `log.critical` and reported a discrepancy but left new entries completely
    UNFROZEN. Reproduced pre-fix: an assigned SPY stock position logs
    `reconcile_untracked_stock_assignment` and `HALT_UNTRACKED` is never written. Fix: the STK
    branch now also appends to `frozen_keys`; its operator-facing message updated to say so.
    DELIBERATELY NOT given the OPT branch's sighting debounce: that exists for an EMPIRICALLY
    OBSERVED position-stream flicker (R5, 2026-07-09, a phantom QQQ row sighted-then-disproved
    twice) — assignment is a discrete overnight broker event, not a stream artifact, and there is
    no equivalent evidence a stock-position sighting flickers the same way. Whether STK should get
    its own debounce, and whether it should route through the Telegram declare-yes/no flow the OPT
    branch uses, is a real design question, left to W51 rather than decided here under a different
    finding's scope.

[5] NEW — `max_contracts_per_trade` startup guard-rail (GOV-6). `settings.py`'s own field default

Second wave of the 2026-09-21 roadmap. Named as four items; re-probing first — this wave's own
instruction — changed the shape of two of them and the scope of a third. Recorded here rather than
silently absorbed, same discipline as the 2026-09-17 REGISTER CORRECTION entry and W41's own
